title: Stepmother and mother
hookLine: court life is a stepmother, philosophy a mother; visit the mother often (Meditations 6.12)
last: GIVE THE PEG A QUICK TWIST.

lines: THE JOB AND THE THING THAT KEEPS YOU SANE.
cards: There's a job, and there's the thing that keeps you sane while you do the job. For some people it's a Sunday morning run. For some it's a prayer before work, or a notebook, or an hour with an old friend.

When life gets loud, that thing can be the first to go. Marcus Aurelius had a court to run: the palace, the petitions, the flatterers. And in book six he gives himself a family picture for how to live with it.

teach.b: Suppose, Marcus says in Meditations six, twelve, you had a stepmother and a mother at the same time. You'd do your duty by your stepmother, but you'd keep going back to your mother. Then he names them.
The court is the stepmother. Philosophy is the mother. A word about the picture: in his sentence the stepmother is the one you owe duty to, and the mother is the one you keep returning to.
That's his picture, not a verdict on stepmothers, and plenty of stepmothers today are deeply loved. What matters is the shape: one relationship you serve faithfully, one that feeds you.
Notice he doesn't tell himself to quit the court. He says be dutiful there; the duty is real. But go back to philosophy often, and rest in her.
And here's the surprise: by doing this, he says, the court will seem bearable to you, and you'll seem bearable in the court.
The visits home don't take him away from his work.
They're what make him fit to do it, and fit to be around. It's like coming home from a hard week to a kitchen where you're simply known.
Read the other way, the line carries a quiet warning: skip the visits long enough, and the court may find you harder to bear.

how: Readers of Marcus often keep a short daily return to reading, reflection or prayer alongside demanding work, treating it as what makes the work bearable rather than as an escape from it.

o: the emperor who served the court but kept going home to philosophy
the emperor who said family must always come before duty
the emperor who left the court to live as a philosopher

games.q: stepmother and mother — tap the pairs.

s: Marcus tells himself to leave the court for philosophy
he tells himself to stay dutiful at court and keep returning to philosophy.
Marcus says returning to philosophy makes him bearable to the court too
the court seems bearable to him, and he to the court.

games.q: you're emperor, buried in court business, and you haven't had a quiet hour in weeks. what does Marcus tell himself?
o: stay dutiful at court, and go back to philosophy often.
give up philosophy until things calm down.
games.why: Meditations 6.12: be dutiful to the stepmother, but return often to your mother and rest in her.

practice: Ask yourself quietly what your mother is, in Marcus's sense: the practice or place or person that feeds you, a walk, a book, prayer, music, maybe this very sit. Without scolding, notice when you last visited.
For the rest of the sit, simply be here, in one of those visits.

wordCard.voice: Marcus, who pictured the court as a stepmother to be served faithfully, and philosophy as the mother he kept returning to. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: mother. Marcus's word for philosophy in 6.12; the stepmother is μητρυιά (may-troo-YAH).

carryVoice: Your line: visit the mother. The visits home make the court bearable. Go gently.
